sentences.text: The largest teaching union had objected to the prospect of partly funding a 3.5% pay increase this year out of existing school budgets Schools in England are to get around £500 million in extra funding towards the teachers' pay award this school year, reducing the risk of a strike ballot by the largest education union.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: Schools had been expected to fund some of the 3.5% teachers pay increase for the current school year out of their existing budgets, which National Education Union (NEU) leaders had strongly objected to.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the NEU, said the offer of more funding was a "significant" step in negotiations.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: In a letter to the union on Wednesday, which has been seen by the BBC, the government said the increase would be funded by savings in employers' contributions to the local government pension scheme.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: The letter said the 4.9 percentage point drop in what employers are expected to contribute will deliver "significant savings" on the pay bill for support staff, which will not be clawed back by central government.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: The National Education Union said it expected the extra money to be around £500m, which schools can now use towards teachers' pay this year.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: In July, ministers accepted the recommendation of the independent pay review body for teachers and agreed a 3.5% increase from September 2026 would be followed by 3% the following year.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: The pay increase had been partly funded by an additional £700m for 2026-27 and £1.1bn for the following year.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: Independent economists at the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that left schools facing a shortfall of around 1% between rising costs and funding this year.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: Luke Sibieta, IFS research fellow, said the extra money would mean the pay increase this year was fully funded - and on top of other funding increases, schools would be £1.6bn better off by next year than they had expected this summer.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: The additional money could potentially bring the uplift for this year into line with next year.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: Kebede said schools has been "running on empty" and the funding signalled "a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community".
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Headteachers, said the decision is "certainly welcome", putting schools in a "better position".
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: He said his union would look carefully at the detail "to determine whether this means the pay uplift is genuinely fully funded" for schools.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said he was "pleased" at the announcement of additional funding but "the wider pressure on school and college budgets remains intense".
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: Similarly, the NASUWT union welcomed the news.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: General secretary Matt Wrack added schools needed "a sustainable, long-term injection of extra funding" to meet the needs of young people.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: In an indicative ballot by the NEU in April, 90% of teachers who voted said they would be prepared to take industrial action over funding and pay, on a turnout of 48%.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: A formal ballot was due to begin on 3 October and close 15 December, raising the prospects of teachers pay strikes early in 2027.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: The national executive of the NEU will meet on 24 September to consider whether to call that off following the additional funding on offer from the government.
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: A spokesperson for Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government was "confident schools can now meet the costs of the award at a national level".
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: Liberal Democrat schools spokesperson Caroline Voaden said she was "glad the government has seen sense, but schools shouldn't have gone through the stress of working out where the money would come from".
sentences.article_title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike

sentences.text: There could be tens of thousands more teenagers who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) than official statistics suggest, the children's commissioner for England has warned.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: A report by Dame Rachel de Souza said around 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England were officially classed as studying at college, but were not showing up at least half of the time.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: She said they had gone "under the radar" and were "not getting the support that they need".
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: The Department for Education (DfE) said it planned to help colleges track attendance and ultimately to gather that data centrally.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: Unlike schools, further education and sixth form colleges in England are not required to collect or report attendance data.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: Dame Rachel's report is based on attendance data obtained from 262 college groups in England and says rates are "substantially lower" than in schools.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: It suggests that more than half (52.2%) of 16- and 17-year-olds are estimated to be persistently absent by the standards used in schools, meaning they are missing 10% or more of college sessions.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: And around 42,000 (5.9%) are severely absent, meaning they are missing at least half of college sessions.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: The DfE estimates that 57,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England are Neet, and Dame Rachel's report argues that these persistently absent teenagers should be considered as "hidden" Neets alongside them.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: Dame Rachel told the BBC a range of factors led to teenagers missing college, including part-time work and travel costs, and that some had been largely absent from education since the Covid pandemic.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: She said while those juggling part-time employment were likely to miss college every so often, it was those who are "far more vulnerable" who were likely to be severely absent.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: She added that it was "shocking" that the DfE did not collect the data as it meant the issue was "ignored".
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: "It's under the radar and these kids are not getting the support that they need," she said.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: One in eight young people still out of work or education ahead of major review Want your job application to stand out?
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: Employers say they look for these six skills Competition for degree apprenticeships quadruples as university costs rise Liam Sloan, principal at Bolton College, said not many students missed more than half of classes, but those who were absent often had mental health challenges or part-time jobs.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: "Sometimes the student being able to be offered that £30 shift there and then means more... than the potential qualification in six or seven months' time," he said.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: He said there was a particular issue in English and maths GCSE classes, which students in England are required to study alongside other courses if they don't have a grade 4 or above.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: Attendance rates at the college had improved in recent years though, he said, and this year it has introduced full-time "positive engagement officers" to greet students each morning and contact those who do not show up.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: In May, the first instalment of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn warned that figure could be one in six within five years, and that the country was "at risk of a lost generation." The final instalment is expected to set out recommendations for tackling the problem in the coming weeks.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: Dame Rachel's report describes "hidden" Neets as those enrolled but persistently absent from college, while Milburn's interim report used it to describe those who are Neet and also not claiming benefits, and are therefore harder to reach.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: Cath Sezen, director of education policy at the Association of Colleges, said she agreed with many of the report's recommendations but said "funding pressures [were] limiting colleges' ability to provide tailored support".
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: "We have called time and time again for increased investment, better integration of support services and a stronger national strategy for employer engagement," she said.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: The DfE said students in further education needed to be prioritised in future reforms to help tackle the Neets crisis.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: A spokesperson also said a new stepping-stone qualification would be brought in to reduce the "endless treadmill" of students failing and resitting GCSE maths and English, and that the government would track attendance in colleges and accelerate the rollout of mental health support teams.
sentences.article_title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns

sentences.text: There will be a boost for fresh fruit and vegetables and deep-fried food will be banned in what the government has called the biggest shake-up to school dinners in England in over a decade.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Under new school food standards, fibre and wholegrains will also be increased, and breakfast clubs will have to follow nutrition rules for the first time, with schools also being monitored.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) welcomed the changes, but said they hoped the new rules would not become "another stick with which to beat head teachers".
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: The changes will come into effect from 2027 and be funded with existing money for schools, the government said.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: As part of the new framework, sweet desserts, like cake, will be reduced from a regular lunch offer to twice a week in secondary schools, and once a week in primary schools.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: They also must now be served with a portion of fruit.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Servings of processed meats such as ham, sausages and chicken nuggets have been reduced to once a week and must come with a side of vegetables or fruit.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Education Secretary Lucy Powell said they were "once-in-a-generation changes" which would "transform school food for children across the country".
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: The Department for Education said it hoped the reforms would tackle childhood obesity, improve nutrition and support children's concentration, learning and wellbeing.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Schools will be required to publish food policies and menus online with monitoring arrangements set to be developed alongside the Food Standards Agency, it said.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Pepe Di'Iasio, ASCL general secretary, said parents would feel "reassured" that schools were providing children with a healthy diet.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: But on plans for enforcement, he added: "None of us would consider ourselves experts in health and nutrition.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Schools Minister Georgia Gould told BBC Breakfast she was confident schools could deliver healthy meals within existing budgets, without diverting funding from elsewhere, like teaching, and that schools would be given a year to implement the changes.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: She said the government was "absolutely determined to support schools" to redesign their menus affordably.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: As part of the changes, deep-fried chips will have to be oven-baked instead, and pasta dishes will need to be 50% wholewheat once a week.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: High-fibre bread will also become a requirement.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Under the new rules, all dishes must come with at least one portion of fruit or vegetables Breakfast clubs will undergo one of the biggest changes.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Historically, there has been no guidance on what they should provide, but from next September pastries and fried-eggs will be off the menu and there will be a sugar cap when it comes to cereals.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: The government said Coco Pops would no longer be an option and chocolate spread was "not permitted".
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Since February this year, 1,250 schools have offered free breakfast clubs to their pupils.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: One of those was Oasis Academy Blakenhale in Birmingham, where principal Farzana Ahmed said the school welcomed the changes.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: "The more children that can access a hot, nutritious meal, the better it is for us, the better it is for them, and actually it really supports families with the reduction of their financial pressures at home," she said.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Ahmed said it was "important" that schools are monitored, but added that they "probably need some more guidance from the government on what that's going to look like on a day-to-day basis".
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: Farzana Ahmed welcomed both the new school food standards and the expansion of free school meals eligibility About 60% of pupils at the inner-city school receive free school meals, and Ahmed said they were already providing a healthy, balanced diet.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: With free school meal eligibility expanding this year to all families who receive Universal Credit , Ahmed said there had been an "influx of parents" applying, and expects around 70% of pupils to benefit going forward.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: "It's a really positive move," she said.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: "He doesn't have to eat those cold sandwiches anymore," she said.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: "By the end of the day he used to be starving.
sentences.article_title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

sentences.text: But now he's coming home all happy because he's having good, healthy meals with a snack as well." Newly-eligible parent Kinza is delighted her children can now have free school dinners The new food standards will apply to primary and secondary schools in England, but rules for school dinners vary across the UK.

sentences.text: The interest rate on those loans is the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation plus up to 3% depending on earnings, and borrowers repay at a rate of 9% of everything they earn over a repayment threshold, which is meant to rise with inflation every year.

sentences.text: The BBC spoke to parents and experts to find out their back-to-school tips It's back-to-school time again - and families brace for the challenge of swapping summer lie-ins for school routines, easing first-day nerves and getting ready for the year ahead.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: While children in Scotland returned to school in mid-August, children in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will be returning in the coming week as September begins.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: We spoke to experts to find out their six key tips to make going back to school as stress-free as possible.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: Cerys Parker, a teacher and blogger, says one of the best ways to keep organised during school time is to keep a consistent morning routine.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: Her morning starts 30 minutes before her children wake up, for some alone time and a hot coffee.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: She  then makes them the same breakfast every morning, which they eat together with no screens, then it's upstairs for showers and getting ready for school.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: Parker also keeps copies of her children's timetables so she knows what to prepare on specific days, such as when they have PE She grabs their lunch boxes and they leave the house at 07:30 for the bus, or 07:50 if Parker is dropping them at school on the way to her own job.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: The night before, she makes sure school bags are packed, shoes are ready, uniform is laid out and lunch is packed for the morning.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "We have things in the same place, so the bags are always in the same location, the keys, and that makes the morning smoother.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: There's no panic about where everything's going to be." It is easy to forget non-uniform days, sports days or study sessions.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: Parker recommends having a family calendar pinned to your wall or your fridge - somewhere you can easily see it every day.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "It's an academic year calendar with a space for each of us, and then an events section, so as soon as a notice comes in, I write it down." This could include things like meal plans, after-school activities or - depending on your child's age - exams.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: After school, many children are tired and are not up for discussion about their day, so Will Shield, professor of child and educational psychology at the University of Exeter, suggests changing your approach to the conversation.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "Ask some open questions, instead of interrogating them," he says.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "Ask what made you smile today?
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: Or who did you play with at lunchtime?" These sorts of questions are a lot easier to answer for a child, he says, instead of asking what they did.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "See it as part of the process of separating and loving you, missing you, which is really important." Many families will have children attending school for the first time, which can be just as big a moment for parents as it is for new pupils.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: Shield says parents should "reassure themselves" about the routine they will need to follow on school mornings.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "Visit the school, walk or drive past it, bring bedtimes back a bit earlier so it's not just a big start in the first week," he says.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "It's about much more basic things, like feeling comfortable and safe to be in a classroom with other children," she says.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: Building independence can also help bridge the gap between home and school life, she says, by encouraging your child to do some things by themselves, such as zipping up their own coat.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "It's just building that sense of, I'm ready to do this without you," she says.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: But Deiros Collado also stresses that your child should be able to ask for help when they need it.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "One of the best skills you can give your little ones is being able to say to an adult, 'Help me,' because you want your kid to be able to say that to a teacher." She also suggests a "goodbye ritual" with your child to practise separation, such as blowing a kiss.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: Katharine Radice says that focusing too much on the homework outcome you want for your child can be "demotivating" for them Katharine Radice, teacher and author, recommends putting together a homework timetable.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "Doing this puts boundaries around homework and makes it easier to ring-fence distraction-free time," she says.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: This could be different every week depending on different activities, but Radice stresses there should be a plan in advance so it's not left to the last minute.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: For supporting children with homework, Radice suggests approaching the task in a "positive and open way" and listening to what they might be finding difficult.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: She also recommends looking for opportunities to praise your child's effort in doing work to help them "stay motivated." "If your child thinks their outcomes won't meet your expectations, they may start to feel that their effort is pointless," she says.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: Some children who are returning to school may have anxieties about the year ahead, and Shield recommends to sit with your child and listen to their concerns.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "Don't immediately reassure them by saying, 'You'll be fine,'" he says.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: "The child's got no evidence they will be fine because they're worried." He suggests phrases such as "I can see you're worried" to make a child feel listened to.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: It is also worth trying to dig deeper to find out what is making them worried about school specifically.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: He also recommends some gentle encouragement of positive things they like about school to ease some worries, such as lunchtime or playing sports with friends.
sentences.article_title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

sentences.text: If anxiety does become overwhelming for them, if they aren't sleeping or it is stopping them from doing everyday things, then Shield recommends talking to the school or a local GP.

sentences.text: Colombia has again topped the list of countries with the highest number of killings of land and environmental activists, according to an annual report by campaign group Global Witness , external .
sentences.article_title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says

sentences.text: Out of at least 124 activists killed globally in 2025, 39 were murdered in Colombia, followed by Brazil with 26.
sentences.article_title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says

sentences.text: Global Witness says that 85% of the documented killings took place in Latin America, making it the deadliest region for every year since the group started publishing its reports in 2012.
sentences.article_title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says

sentences.text: Most of the killings were part of land disputes and in many cases they were carried out by hitmen or members of organised crime gangs, the report states.
sentences.article_title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says

sentences.text: Colombia has accounted for the highest number of murders of environmental activists for the past four years.
sentences.article_title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says

sentences.text: Almost half of those killed in the country were members of indigenous groups, while many of the remaining ones were small-scale farmers, Global Witness's report says.
sentences.article_title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says

sentences.article_title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says

sentences.article_title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says

sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: The BBC's defence correspondent explains what the US announcement means The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Washington has given away little in its announcement.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: So what could this weapon be, and what is the wider picture like for military developments in space?
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Who else could have similar weaponry?
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Space has been a militarised domain since the start of the space age - in the late 1960s, the Soviet Union deployed weapons up there.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: The Istrebitel Sputnikov (IS; Satellite Destroyer) programme was made up of satellites that were designed to release projectiles that detonated, releasing shrapnel into the path of another (usually American) satellite.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Nowadays, advanced militaries deploy satellites in space for a range of purposes, including reconnaissance, secure communications, detecting missile launches and providing precise location information for targeted strikes.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: As warfare becomes more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Some types of space weaponry could create a lot of debris and destruction Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless." Bowen also would not rule out a riskier and more disruptive type of weaponry, which could create debris and destruction.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: A type of "close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well." As to whether rivals such as Russia and China have similar weaponry already in orbit, is difficult to tell.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "If we're looking towards China and Russia, they have both displayed activity," Juliana Suess, a former research fellow at RUSI and researcher at the Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (German Institute for International and Security Affairs), told the BBC.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "For example, with Russia, we've seen some activity that hints at being a co-orbital weapons test.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: So we saw something that might indicate that they shot a projectile as a test in orbit.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: In a later BBC interview, Bowen was dismissive of China's reaction to the US announcement which warned against an arms race in space, describing it as "the pot calling the kettle black".
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "If you're already an expert... you know how hollow those words are coming from the Russian and Chinese governments," he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "The United States, Russia and China and also India have all developed different kinds of anti-satellite or counter-space weapons, and Russia and China have put a lot of technologies in space which have a lot of weapons potential," he added.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: In fact in the past 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "Theoretically, these RPO [satellites]can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Bowen added that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit." This, he said, could be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: However, some types of space weaponry also have the potential to create huge amounts of space junk.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Dr Mark Hilborne, a specialist in space security and weaponisation at King's College,  said direct ascent anti-satellite missile tests, such as one carried out by China in 2007, leave a great deal of debris in orbit for a very long time.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Suess said debris from that test was still in orbit and still dangerous.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "It doesn't have to be a sort of huge piece of metal to do any damage, it can be a tiny piece of plastic, given the velocity that we're talking about in orbit," she said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Thornton said that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike [satellites] in low Earth orbit.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: They also have ASAT [air-launched antisatellite] missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Only if it was happening on the ground as well.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "What could happen in space is not something that would happen in isolation, really," Bowen said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "Nothing could happen, or something could." This video can not be played Watch: US Space Force Guardians spring into action during training exercise Given that weapons for use in space have been around for so long, why did the US announcement come when it did?
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Experts agree that it's not a major development as such, more a political signal.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Bowen suggested that it could be a response to Chinese developments.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "China has modernised its military forces over the past 30 years," he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Thornton said that, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, because it has so few satellites, unlike China and the US.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: It would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring satellites designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers," he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Professor Dave Chadwick from Bangor University sampling damaged remains following wildfires at Mynydd Llangynidr in Bannau Brycheiniog Scientists investigating the damage caused by severe wildfires across Wales this summer say the impact has been "catastrophic".
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: Extreme heat and exceptionally dry conditions throughout July and August left landscapes such as heathland, moorland and upland grasslands vulnerable to fast spreading fires, resulting in one of the UK's worst wildfire seasons in recent years.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: Prof Davey Jones, who is leading a Bangor University survey of several sites across Wales, said the scale of damage was far greater than what was immediately visible.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "People see the blackened vegetation and assume that's the main impact, but the real story is below our feet," said Jones.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: During the July peak, fires affected approximately 2,760 acres of countryside across north Wales alone, the equivalent of more than 1,500 football pitches.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: At Sychnant Pass in Conwy county, one of the most significant blazes saw 36 homes having to be evacuated and about 200 acres of land affected.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: Prof Davey Jones said the scale of damage from the wildfires was far greater than what was immediately visible At Sychnant Pass today, there are slight green shoots of recovery visible among the charred hillside.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: But Jones described a rare ecosystem housing specialist plants, butterflies and insects, "where the UK is the epicentre globally".
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "We've probably lost about 10 centimetres of soil here [at Sychnant Pass] so we've lost all of that organic matter layer... 4,000 years of carbon gone in a single event," he said.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "Once the topsoil is gone, we can never recover that.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "People see the blackened vegetation and assume that's the main impact, but the real story is below our feet.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "This soil acts as a water sponge, a carbon store, a nutrient bank.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "Losing it is a double whammy, it worsens climate change and makes the habitat far more fragile." He added: "This site has taken thousands of years to develop and it's all gone in maybe five days?
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "If we are going to try and put that soil back, generate artificial soils through the reuse of organic wastes for example, then it's important we understand what the soil quality is now.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "So that we can prepare for the future and design those soils, because they don't exist yet." Over recent weeks the Bangor team has been racing to collect soil samples at several sites across Wales before heavy winter rainfall washes away the remains.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: Their work has included comparing the burnt land with adjacent untouched areas, allowing researchers to measure changes in soil carbon, nutrients, microbial activity, water repellency and erosion risk.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: Even NASA satellite data has been used to quickly identify new sites after fires have occurred.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: Dr Kara Marsden says responding quickly is key Dr Kara Marsden, a lecturer in soil science who is also working on the project, said working at speed was vital.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "It was really important that we got on site very quickly to measure the soil and vegetation properties while the fire's impacts were still fresh," she said.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "These things can change rapidly, so capturing that baseline data now means we'll have something accurate to compare against in future sampling dates." She warned that early green shoots now visible at the site did not necessarily reflect true or full recovery.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "Bracken sprouts almost immediately because its rhizomes sit deep in the soil, so the burn layer wouldn't maybe have impacted those" she said.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "But the heather and gorse have much shallower roots, so you know they're completely gone.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "They've been completely lost... that depth of soil they depend on could take thousands of years to form again." Jones said that the impact of such wildfires extended far beyond biodiversity loss.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "Fires release carbon, nitrogen and sulphur back into the atmosphere, in itself contributing to climate change," he said.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "Every time we have a wildfire, we're just making the problem worse and worse.
sentences.article_title: Summer wildfires caused catastrophic hidden damage, scientists warn

sentences.text: "It becomes a self‑sustaining cycle... drier soils, more fires, more carbon released." He also warned that without rapid restoration and better wildfire preparedness, "we might lose pretty much all of this habitat within our lifetime".

sentences.text: A series of social media adverts for AI apps have been banned by a UK watchdog for promoting "the creation of sexually explicit content and objectification of women".
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said five ads uploaded to Meta platforms for AI companion and video generating apps had objectified and sexualised women, including through harmful gender stereotypes.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: One of the ads used sexualised images of a girl under 18 to promote an AI companion app - while others invited users to upload images of their "crush" and turn images into "sizzling" videos.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: Meta had already removed the offending ads.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: But Nicky Baker of the ASA said such content had the potential "to cause real-world harm".
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: "We take a firm line on ads that are likely to cause serious or widespread offence and these ads are a clear example of why that matters," she said.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: "Encouraging and condoning the objectification of women and the creation of explicit content from people's images has the potential to cause real-world harm." The ASA also said many of the ads it banned had promoted the creation of sexually explicit content using real women's images without their consent.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: It comes only months after the UK outlawed apps to create non-consensual deepfake nude imagery - sparked by outrage over X's chatbot Grok complying with requests to nudify images of women on the platform .
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: The ASA said the law had changed during its investigations and that ads identified in future would be considered in light of both the law and its own rules.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: Where ads are identified as illegal, it said it may notify platforms and law enforcement.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: The ads were identified by the regulator using its AI-powered "Active Ad Monitoring System", which proactively searches for ads which might violate UK rules.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: It said the five ads it were banned had depicted women irresponsibly, and were likely to cause serious or widespread offence.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: One ad for an AI companion generator, developed by Animcha Ltd, was also found to have portrayed someone under 18 in a sexual way, the ASA said.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: It presented the synthetic female character as someone users could "customise" and instruct, combining sexualised imagery with childlike clothing and objects.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: Two ads for an AI portrait generation tool called Nexaipic encouraged users to "upload your crush and let AI create what you imagine" with sexually explicit videos.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: An ad for an AI image-to-video generation app, identified only as KH31 DD22, depicted a clothed woman being transformed into a video in which she was topless.

sentences.text: The watchdog said this suggested the app could be used to create content that exposed women's bodies.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: Further adverts for image generation tool Rusto AI, which encouraged users to create sexualised videos from photographs, were found to have condoned the digital manipulation of women's images to create sexually explicit content.
sentences.article_title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog

sentences.text: And an ad for an AI image-to-video generation app PictoPop used sexualised imagery to demonstrate the tool, including by portraying the woman in a submissive position.

sentences.text: The boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI says people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe, amid rising public concerns about the risks.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: "The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: He accepted people were justified in being concerned about AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: But critics say firms cannot be trusted to self-regulate, with left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, among those calling for greater governance of AI.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: Trump himself has criticised calls for more guardrails on the fast-moving technology, calling fears about AI's safety a "hoax".
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: He said the only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: Altman's comments on Tuesday came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: "It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: "I think the world is right to be afraid of this." But AI bosses themselves have also admitted it may be difficult to regulate a technology which is changing so quickly.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: In an interview with Axios published on 3 September , external , Altman said he had expected Congress to create a "basic framework" for advanced AI after his 2023 testimony, but that has yet to happen.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: He suggested lawmakers have struggled to keep pace with the technology and to regulate it without "slow[ing] down innovation".
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: New safety legislation on AI is unlikely to emerge from the US Congress anytime soon, despite the fact lawmakers returned from their summer break on Monday.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: There is a lack of consensus within both US parties on how any regulation would happen - and the House is set to enter recess again at the end of the week ahead of the midterm elections in early November.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings Altman's comments on Tuesday were the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: The researcher claimed AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade if left unchecked.
sentences.article_title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

sentences.text: A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.

sentences.text: David Etor's first break came after designing and building a kind of "solar oven" in Nigeria A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in the School of Electrical, Electronic and Mechanical Engineering at the University of Bristol.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our dignity" in front of neighbours.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: "I didn't see a way out," he said.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his memoir, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: "It was a very poor neighbourhood.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: "I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: "[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: "She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: To solve the problem, he designed and built a kind of "solar oven".
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: "It worked incredibly well," he said, which led to an award from the state government and a job.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: That subsequently led him to receive a scholarship to study electrical power at Newcastle University and a PhD at Durham University, before he secured his current job in Bristol.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: Sir Steve Webb, the former MP and Pensions Minister, who got to know Etor through the church in Bristol, called his achievements "remarkable".
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: "David's message is very much that people shouldn't be defined by their upbringing or their background," he said.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: "They shouldn't be written off." "I was pinching myself on my way here this morning," Etor added.
sentences.article_title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'

sentences.text: Caballas is a nickname for the people of Ceuta - a Spanish autonomous city on the North African coast, bordering Morocco and separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar.
sentences.article_title: Mbappe says he 'stands with Ceuta' after T-shirt row

sentences.text: More than 100 people died when tens of thousands of migrants crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in July.
sentences.article_title: Mbappe says he 'stands with Ceuta' after T-shirt row

sentences.text: The Mercator projection is the map widely used across the globe but inaccurately depicts the sizes of countries and continents The UN has just called for the predominant world map to be replaced with one that more accurately reflects the true size of continents such as Africa.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy with the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The UN adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The Mercator projection has been around since the 16th Century and was vital for navigating the oceans The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University College London explained.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: "He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well." To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are and countries nearer the poles appear stretched.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: "Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The Equal Earth map aims to represent landmasses' area more fairly The Equal Earth map aims to address this problem with the Mercator projection.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: It was developed by a team of cartographers in 2018 to present the size and shape of landmasses more accurately, and was inspired by the 1963 Robinson projection - a map that shows the entire globe's surface at once.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: As a result, the Equal Earth map was adopted by African Union members in February, before it was adopted by the UN.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: But it sacrifices the straight lines that made the Mercator projection perfect for navigating with - and it cannot be used for measuring the true distance between different places.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: "You can preserve area, or you can preserve shape, or you can preserve distance and direction, but not everything at once perfectly, because otherwise you'd be back to a sphere," Cheshire said.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The Peters map projection gives a fairer idea of land area but distorts shape The Peters world map was designed by German historian Arno Peters in the early 1970s.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The rectangular map is based on the projection first described by Scottish cartographer James Gall in 1855.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The projection sacrifices accuracy of shape in favour of accuracy of scale.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: So, polar regions are squished, while the bits near the equator are stretched.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: This fixes the Greenland-Africa size issue, allowing those who use it to get a sense of the comparative size of different landmasses, all while preserving straight lines of longitude and latitude.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: However, the map severely distorts the shapes of Earth's landmasses, making them all look slightly off.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: Russia, for instance, looks much smaller than it actually is.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The straight lines on the Peters map also do not represent true constant compass bearings and so are useless for navigation.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: This Mercator projection puts the Americas front and centre instead of Europe and Africa In the same way the apparent size of a landmass can influence its perceived importance, so can its prominence on a map.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: Some cartographers have attempted to orient the map so the south is at the top, to counter the psychological bias that comes from the global south being viewed as less imporant because it's lower down.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: And depending on where you are in the world, which continent is placed in the centre of a map can vary.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: While these alternate maps offer a different perspective on the world to the one we may be familiar with, they don't solve the issue of prominence, but rather simply change the focus of a map.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The UN flag is centred on the North Pole so no one continent is the primary focus One way of resolving the issue of which landmass is at the centre of a map - and therefore the most prominent - is putting none of them at the centre.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: This is what the map in the UN logo does: the world is centred around the North Pole, with the continents radiating outward from it.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: It's known as an "Azimuthal equidistant projection", placing world regions on a circular map around a focal point.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: The further away from that point on the globe, the bigger the circle.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: On this type of map, all points are at the correct "azimuth" - or horizontal direction - from the centre point.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: But to fit the entire surface of a sphere onto a circle, the map becomes more distorted the further away from the centre it gets.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: On the UN map, for instance, areas near the South Pole appear squished and stretched as what would be a ring of the same circumference as one around the North Pole becomes much larger.
sentences.article_title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

sentences.text: Instead, the Partick Thistle duo are in line to play for Uganda.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: They believe they would become the first white players ever to represent the African nation, thanks to their mother Kate being born there.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: "My gran and grandad lived out here for, I think, four or five years," Olly, 18, tells BBC Sport Scotland.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: "My grandfather came out here to teach in a school then my mum was born here.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: So, it's a bit of a strange one." The siblings became aware of interest from Uganda about six months ago, following a chance conversation some time before between their father and a football consultant at a game in Nigeria.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: And, at the start of August, they were invited to attend under-20 and under-17s training camps.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: They spent last week in Jinja in the country's eastern region and will stay on for one more week, with the pair saying they're "shocked" and "honoured" at the call-ups.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: "I couldn't believe it," 16-year-old striker Seb said.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: "It's one of those things you look at and you're shocked.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: Most other people couldn't as well." Goalkeeper Olly had a similar reaction.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: "A real mixture of emotions," he said.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: I didn't really think that this was a possibility but I was honoured to be asked to represent Uganda.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: I thought it was a real big opportunity." Mum Kate is "ecstatic" and "thinks it'd be a great experience for us", adds Seb.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: Olly Fisher, second right, with his Ugandan team-mates There is another Scottish link with Uganda, with former Hearts and Ghana midfielder Laryea Kingston currently coach of Uganda's under-20s.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: And he is the one who believes the Fisher brothers are on the verge of making history.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: "Coach Kingston was saying we'd be the first white boys to play for Uganda, which would be history in the making," Seb explained.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: And even though they have been training in oppressively warm conditions, they are embracing the opportunity.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: "Everyone has been brilliant, welcoming, really great," Seb said.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: "The other boys have been brand new with us.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: Some of the boys actually come from the same area where my mum was born.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: So, they were all talking about that." The boys will return to Scotland soon, combining training and playing with Thistle with university and school, but are planning to rejoin their new international team-mates in the near future.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda

sentences.text: "That's what you want as a footballer, being in an international environment," Seb said.
sentences.article_title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda
